title: the departure
hook: before he leaves, Rama gives everything away, and makes a poor old man throw his stick

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's rage and restraint, complete. A bow, a spade and a basket, and Urmila left in silence. Did you give one frustration a job? Today the departure begins, with giving. Day five hundred thirty-one.
screen: `A BOW, A SPADE AND A BASKET.`

segments.voice: When people move far away, there's usually a day of giving things away. The couch goes to a cousin, the books to a neighbor, the plants to whoever will water them. It's sad and oddly freeing at once. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana have one of those days before they leave. Except what they're giving away is the wealth of a prince. And in the middle of it, Valmiki tells a small story with a joke in it, which is not what you'd expect on the worst day of Rama's life.
screen: `A DAY OF GIVING THINGS AWAY.` → `A PRINCE'S WEALTH.` → `A JOKE ON THE WORST DAY.`

segments.voice: Rama sends for Suyajna, the son of his teacher Vasishtha, and gives him armlets, earrings and jewels. Sita sends a necklace and a golden girdle to Suyajna's wife. Gifts go to teachers, to the brahmins who taught the princes, to the old servants of the household, to people who depend on Rama for their living, so that nobody is left without support while he's gone. Then the story. Near Ayodhya lives a very poor brahmin named Trijata. He's old and thin and spends his days digging in the fields with a spade, scraping a living. His wife, hearing that Rama is giving things away, says to him: go. Maybe he'll give you something. So Trijata comes and stands before the prince. And Rama, of all things, teases him. I haven't given away even one of my thousand cows yet, he says. Throw your staff. However far it lands, every cow up to that point is yours. The old man ties up his clothes, swings his staff with every bit of strength he has, and throws. It flies across the river Sarayu and lands in a pasture full of cattle. Rama embraces him and gives him every cow up to that spot. And then he apologizes. Don't be offended, he says. It was a joke. I only wanted to see the strength in you. It's a tiny scene. But look at what it shows. On the day his life is falling apart, Rama is still generous, still playful, still paying attention to one poor man's dignity. Grief hasn't made him small.
screen: `GIFTS SO NO ONE IS LEFT WITHOUT.` · `TRIJATA, OLD, POOR, WITH A SPADE.` · `THROW YOUR STAFF.` · `IT WAS A JOKE. FORGIVE ME.` · then, large: `GRIEF HASN'T MADE HIM SMALL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Look around in your mind at what you own: the room you're in, the things on the shelves. Pick one thing you could give away this week, to someone who'd use it. Picture handing it over. Notice how it feels to let it go. Then rest in the breath, lighter by one thing. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part one: giving. Rama and Sita give away their wealth, and Rama makes poor Trijata throw his staff, and gives him every cow up to where it lands.
Your line: the departure. Today, give one thing away, and if you can, make the person laugh while you do it. Day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Giving gifts, dana, before a journey or a major change of life is a long-standing Hindu practice; storytellers often enjoy the Trijata episode as a light moment in a dark book.

tells him to go to Rama

myth: Rama is too grief-stricken to give anything away
he and Sita give generously to teachers, servants and the poor.
Trijata's staff lands across the Sarayu
and Rama gives him every cow up to that spot.

fork.setup: you're Trijata, old and poor. a prince tells you to throw your staff: every cow up to where it lands is yours. what do you do?
options: toss it politely a few feet.
tie up your clothes and throw with all your strength.
fork.reveal: he throws with everything he has, the staff flies across the Sarayu, and Rama gives him the cows, then apologizes for the joke.

original.note: Sanskrit dāna: giving, a gift; one of the most praised acts in Hindu ethics.

trapdoor: what you thought: the departure is all tears.
what it means: it begins with generous giving, and even a joke.
what a scholar hears: it is one of the very few comic moments in the Ayodhya Kanda, and readers often point to it to show that Valmiki's Rama can tease, and apologize.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 32 (gifts to Suyajna and others; Trijata and the staff)
